erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Ya no he terminado el horario.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Todavía no he terminado el horario.

explicacion.en: English speakers often translate “not yet” as ya no. But ya no means “no longer”. For “not yet” use todavía no.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Acabo de empiezo en el puesto.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Acabo de empezar en el puesto.

explicacion.en: After acabar de you always use the infinitive: acabo de empezar, acabas de llegar. The verb acabar itself carries the person and the tense.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: ¿Sabes que ya soy coordinadora, señora Rosa?
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: ¿Sabe que ya soy coordinadora, señora Rosa?

explicacion.en: With señora Rosa you use usted, so the question is ¿Sabe que…? and ¿Le conté que…?, not the tú forms.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: ¿Sabes que Daniela se gradúa en julio?

explicacion.en: English often drops “that” (“Do you know Daniela graduates in July?”), but Spanish always keeps que after sabes.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: La directora propuso me el puesto.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: La directora me propuso el puesto.

explicacion.en: The pronoun me goes before the conjugated verb: me propuso, not propuso me.

texto.en: In English you say “Guess what?”, “Did you know…?” or “It turns out that…”. Spanish has matching openers, and after que the verb is in the ordinary indicative. ¿Sabes que…? asks if the listener already knows the news: ¿Sabes que Daniela se gradúa en julio? ¿Te conté que…? checks whether you already told them: ¿Te conté que soy la nueva coordinadora? Here conté is the yo form of the past of contar (to tell); learn it as part of the phrase. Resulta que… introduces a fact that is surprising or unexpected, like “It turns out that…”: Resulta que la directora me propuso el puesto. It has nothing to do with the English “it results”. Always keep que: English can drop “that”, Spanish cannot.

titulo.en: With usted, and for very recent news

texto.en: With a person you address as usted (señora Rosa, don Jorge, doña Carmen) the openers change: ¿Sabe que…? and ¿Le conté que…? (le instead of te). To talk about recent news you already know three tools. Ya means “already” and todavía no means “not yet”, usually with the present perfect: Ya he terminado el horario. Todavía no he terminado el horario. Acabar de + infinitive means “to have just done something”: Acabo de empezar en el puesto (I just started in the position). Spanish normally uses the present of acabar for this meaning: say acabo de, not acabé de.

titulo.en: The present subjunctive: what it is

texto.en: Until now your verbs were in the indicative, the mood that states facts. The subjunctive is a second set of endings that Spanish uses when the speaker does not state a fact but expresses a hope, a wish or a feeling. Today you meet it in the frame Espero que + subjunctive (I hope that…). The person who hopes and the person who acts are different: Espero que hables con el equipo (I hope that you speak with the team). English can say “I hope you speak” and can drop “that”. Spanish always keeps que and always uses the subjunctive after espero que.

titulo.en: How to form it with regular verbs

texto.en: Take the yo form of the present, drop the -o and add the “opposite” vowel. Verbs in -ar take -e: hablo → hable, hables, hable, hablemos, hablen. Verbs in -er and -ir take -a: como → coma, comas, coma, comamos, coman; vivo → viva, vivas, viva, vivamos, vivan. The usted form is the same as él/ella and the ustedes form is the same as ellos/ellas. You already know these forms: they are the usted and ustedes commands you learned before (Lea el horario, Lean el horario).

To keep the sound of the stem, some -ar verbs change their spelling before the e: c → qu (buscar → busque), g → gu (llegar → llegue) and z → c (organizar → organice). The u in busque and llegue is silent: it only keeps the c and the g hard. Pronounce llegue “YEH-geh”, with a g as in “go”.

contexto.en: The first week of Emma's new job as coordinator at the institute in La Mariscal. Andrés Vaca and Sofía Herrera welcome her. Everyone uses tú.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días, Emma. Bienvenida a tu primera semana como coordinadora. Espero que te guste el puesto.

traduccion.en: Good morning, Emma. Welcome to your first week as coordinator. I hope you like the position.

dialogo.texto: Gracias, Andrés. Espero que trabajemos bien juntos.

traduccion.en: Thank you, Andrés. I hope we work well together.

dialogo.texto: Seguro. Vas a coordinar y dirigir el equipo de profesores.

traduccion.en: Of course. You are going to coordinate and lead the team of teachers.

dialogo.texto: Es un equipo grande. Espero que todos colaboren.

traduccion.en: Thanks, Sofía. I'm going to arrive at eight. I hope you also arrive on time.

titulo.en: Reacting to news with ¡Qué bueno que…!

texto.en: To react to news Spanish uses ¡Qué + adjective + que…! followed by the subjunctive: ¡Qué bueno que Daniela termine la carrera! (How great that Daniela is finishing her degree!). The subjunctive appears because you are giving your feeling about the news, not announcing it, even when the news is true. In English the verb stays in the ordinary present (“finishes”); in Spanish it must be termine. The present subjunctive covers what is happening now or will happen soon: ¡Qué bueno que termines en julio! The adjective stays bueno: it does not agree with the person, so do not say ¡Qué buena que…!

Change the key word to change the feeling: ¡Qué bien que…! (How nice that…!) and ¡Qué lástima que…! (What a shame that…!). To congratulate you can say ¡Felicidades! or ¡Felicitaciones! on their own, or use the verb felicitar with a pronoun before it. With tú: ¡Te felicito! With usted: ¡Lo felicito! to a man and ¡La felicito! to a woman. The pronoun goes before the verb. To congratulate someone for something use por: ¡Te felicito por tu título!
Words and phrases you will meet in the examples and the dialogue.

texto.en: Some of the most useful verbs do not follow the plain rule, so learn them as a group: tener → tenga, hacer → haga, ir → vaya, ser → sea, estar → esté, saber → sepa and poder → pueda. Tener and hacer are irregular because their yo form is irregular (tengo, hago): drop the -o, add -a, and the g stays: tenga, haga. Poder keeps its stem change in every form except nosotros: pueda, puedas, pueda, podamos, puedan. Four verbs are truly irregular: ir (vaya), ser (sea), saber (sepa) and estar (esté, with accents on all forms except estemos). Except for estar, which keeps the -ar endings (-é, -és, -é, -emos, -én), the endings are the ones you know: -a, -as, -a, -amos, -an.

Verbs whose yo form ends in -go keep that g in the subjunctive: salgo → salga, vengo → venga, digo → diga, tengo → tenga, hago → haga. You do not need a new rule: drop the -o of the yo form and add the opposite vowel, as you learned before. The yo form is already irregular, so the subjunctive is too.

titulo.en: Using them with espero que and ¡Qué bueno que…!

texto.en: The new forms work exactly like the regular ones. Espero que todo esté listo. ¡Qué bueno que puedas venir! Notice ser and estar: use estar for a state (todo esté listo) and ser for where an event takes place (la fiesta sea en la casa). In English you say “I hope Mateo can come”; in Spanish Mateo’s verb must be in the subjunctive: pueda.

explicacion.en: English puts “you” after the verb, but in Spanish the pronoun goes before it: que te vaya, que le vaya, que les vaya.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: ¡Que tenga buen viaje, don Jorge!

explicacion.en: With don Jorge you use usted, so the verb is tenga (the same form as él). Tengas is for tú.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: ¡Que descanses!

explicacion.en: The wish uses the subjunctive: -ar verbs take -es for tú. Descansas is the ordinary present.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: ¡Que le vaya bien, don Jorge!

explicacion.en: Les is for several people (ustedes). For one person you address as usted, use le: ¡Que le vaya bien!

texto.en: To wish someone well Spanish starts with que and puts the verb in the subjunctive: ¡Que te vaya bien! (literally “May it go well for you”). There is no main verb: it is as if you had said “I hope that…” or “I wish that…” and left it out. You will hear these wishes at every goodbye: ¡Que tengas suerte! (Good luck!), ¡Que descanses! (Get some rest!), ¡Que lo pases bien! (Have a good time!), ¡Que disfrutes! (Enjoy!), ¡Que tengas buen viaje! (Have a good trip!). You can also say it with a verb: Te deseo mucho éxito (I wish you a lot of success).

Choose the form that matches the person: ¡Que te vaya bien! with tú, ¡Que le vaya bien! with one person you call usted and ¡Que les vaya bien! with a group (ustedes). The verb changes too: ¡Que tengas suerte! (tú), ¡Que tenga suerte! (usted), ¡Que tengan suerte! (ustedes). Emma uses usted with señora Rosa and don Jorge, and tú with Daniela and Mateo.

In these wishes the pronouns te, le and les come before the verb: Que te vaya, que le vaya, que les vaya. They mean “for you”, so the wish is that things go well for that person. In ¡Que lo pases bien! the word lo means “it”, the time you spend: ¡Que lo pases bien! literally means “May you spend it well”.

contexto.en: Graduation day: the ceremony at the university has just ended. Emma, Daniela, Rosa, Jorge and Mateo say goodbye. Emma uses usted with Rosa and Jorge, and tú with Daniela and Mateo.
